extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of language, and classification
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and criteria for forming classes and predicating general names (the Aristotelian 'predicables'): genus, species, differentia, proprium, and accidens; when a class counts as a real 'kind' and how connotation/technical usage affects classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of classes by general names
rubrics_metrics.description: By every general name which we introduce, we create a class, if there be any things, real or imaginary, to compose it; classes mostly owe their existence to general language, though sometimes language owes its existence to classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When we employ a name to connote attributes, the things which possess those attributes are constituted a class; but in predicating the name we predicate only the attributes, not class-membership. Names introduced for convenience of thought (e.g., scientific groupings) do not differ in mode of signification from other connotative names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between predication and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Predication does not presuppose classification: predicating a general name asserts attributes, and class-membership may not come into view at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate the act of predicating attributes with asserting a classificatory scheme. Introducing a general name can incidentally produce a class, but the logical operation of predication is about connoted attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The five predicables (genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens)
rubrics_metrics.description: General names (predicates) may be related to a subject in five ways: as a genus, species, differentia, proprium, or accidens; these are relative terms expressing the relation between predicate and subject on a particular occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single name may serve different predicable roles depending on the subject (e.g., 'animal' is genus relative to man, species relative to Substance). Treat these terms as relational, not as fixed properties of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus and species — popular vs Aristotelian/rigorous senses
rubrics_metrics.description: In popular use any inclusive/exclusive class pair may be called genus and species; Aristotelians restricted genus/species to classes of the 'essence' of the subject (real Kinds) and required proximate (infima) species for the lowest kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit which sense you use. In popular classification many groupings count as genera/species; in rigorous logical usage, only classes distinguished by an indeterminate multitude of properties (Kinds) qualify. Examples: animal/man (popular and Aristotelian), biped (popular genus but not Aristotelian genus relative to man).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlimited power of framing classes; purpose-sensitive selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Any attribute that some things have and others lack can ground a division and hence a class — the number of possible classes is boundless — but the usefulness and depth of those classes vary and depend on purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some classes (e.g., color-based) have only the connoted property in common, while others (e.g., animal) admit an inexhaustible set of common properties. Classification choices should consider whether the distinction marks a real Kind (important, pervasive differences) or is merely convenient for a particular purpose (scientific convenience legitimizes technical connotation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for a 'real Kind' (essential difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'real Kind' (genus or species in the rigorous sense) is distinguished from other classes by an indeterminate multitude of properties not derivable from one another; differences of kind are those that pervade many (perhaps infinite) properties rather than being finite and determinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to judge whether a classification marks a fundamental division (Kind) or an arbitrary/secondary split. If a proposed class is merely characterized by a finite list of properties (e.g., color), it is not a real Kind in the Aristotelian sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximate (infima) species and inclusion of properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The proximate or lowest Kind to which an individual is referrible (its infima species) has properties that necessarily include the whole of the common properties of every other real Kind to which the individual can be referred; other Kinds predicable of the individual stand to the proximate Kind as genera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying the proximate species, ensure it is the nearest Kind whose connoted properties encompass the properties of any broader Kinds that also include the individual. Use this to determine hierarchical relations among classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentia defined as the surplus connotation of a species
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentia is that part of the connotation of the specific name which distinguishes the species from all other species of the same genus: the surplus of connotation the species has over the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentia depends on the classificatory purpose and may be ordinary or technical. The same species may have different differentiae under different classificatory schemes (e.g., 'man' might connote rationality ordinarily but specific dental/structural features in a Linnaean system). When defining a species, state the intended differentia explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprium (property) as a necessary but non-connoted attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: A proprium is an attribute belonging to all individuals of a species which, though not connoted by the name, follows necessarily from connoted attributes; it may follow by demonstration (logical consequence) or by causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish propria from differentiae and accidents: a proprium is not part of the definition but is inescapably true of the species (e.g., equal opposite sides of a parallelogram). Note both kinds (demonstrative and causal) when assessing necessary consequences of a definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidens (accident) and its subclasses (inseparable vs separable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidens includes all attributes neither involved in the signification of the name nor known to be necessarily connected; inseparable accidents are universal in practice but not necessary (e.g., blackness of crows known so far), while separable accidents are sometimes absent or not constant (e.g., color of Europeans, being born).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify non-essential properties carefully: inseparable accidents may appear universal given current knowledge but remain logically non-essential; separable accidents vary across individuals or time. Avoid treating accidents as defining features of a species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/ordinary connotation and the flexibility of definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Words not otherwise connotative may acquire special or technical connotation for classification purposes; the connotation of a term in a particular treatise or discipline may differ from its ordinary meaning and thereby alter which attributes count as differentia or proprium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating definitions/classifications, explicitly record whether terms are used in ordinary or specialized senses. A technical connotation is legitimate when justified by purpose or scientific convenience; be alert to potential ambiguities arising from dual meanings.
